title: How do you lead a case by proposing the next step?
description: Interviewers score whether you drive. Waiting to be told what to do loses candidate-led cases. What to do, what to say, and the mistake to avoid.
hook: Leading the case means you decide where to go next, out loud, with a reason. It is what separates a good candidate from a great one in candidate-led cases. Here is how to do it.
body:
Stage 5 of 10 in the ten stages of a case.

Why it matters

Interviewers score whether you drive. Waiting to be told what to do loses candidate-led cases.

The common mistake

Ending answers with "where would you like me to go next?"

What to do, and what to say

Propose, don’t wait

After your structure and after every answer, say where you want to go next, what data you need, and why. In interviewer-led cases (common at McKinsey) the interviewer picks the next question, but still say what you would look at and why.

"As a next step, I’d like market data to test whether the decline is industry-wide. Do we have anything on that?"

Summarise at the turns

When you finish one area, summarise in two lines and steer.

"Let me quickly summarise where we are: we know A and B; the open question is C."

Practise the moment

Read the situation and say your answer out loud before you open the model.

You’ve just answered a question about costs. Keep driving the case.

Show a strong answer

"So higher delivery-app commissions explain most of the margin drop. As a next step I’d like to see profit per order by channel, to test whether delivery orders make money after commission. Do we have that?"

Why it works: Finding, next step, data needed, and why. Every time.

You’ve covered two of your three buckets. Summarise and steer.

Show a strong answer

"Let me quickly summarise where we are: we know the market is attractive and our product can compete. The open question is whether the economics work, so I’d like to look at the investment needed."

Why it works: Mini-summaries keep the interviewer with you and keep you oriented.

Next stage: charts and exhibits.
outro: Read it once, then try it on a practice case today while it is fresh. One real attempt teaches more than three re-reads. All ten stages, with every phrase, are on the free perfect casing page.
